drill.title: Timed brunoise
body: A brunoise shows every flaw in your knife work. Today you time it, then check it.
steps: Hone your chef's knife and set the board on a damp towel.
Start a timer. Peel one carrot, square it into a block, and cut ⅛-inch planks, then ⅛-inch julienne, then ⅛-inch cubes.
Stop the timer and write down the time.
Spread 20 cubes on the board and measure a few with a ruler. Note how many are within a hair of ⅛ inch.
Repeat with a second carrot and compare the time and the count.
Weigh the trim and the brunoise. Save the trim for stock.
Use the brunoise in this week's fried rice or ratatouille.

quiz.q: What comes before a brunoise?
Which matters first, speed or evenness?
Why square the carrot into a block?
choices: Flat sides make even planks and it can't roll
quiz.explain: And the trim goes to stock.

knowledge.title: Cuts by size: brunoise, small dice, batonnet, chiffonade; the French herb base
body: Professional recipes name cuts by size, so every cook produces the same piece. Learn them as numbers.
Brunoise: ⅛-inch cubes, cut from a julienne. Small dice: ¼-inch cubes, cut from a batonnet. Medium dice: ½ inch. Large dice: ¾ inch.
Julienne: ⅛ by ⅛ inch, 2 to 2½ inches long. Batonnet: ¼ by ¼ inch, 2½ to 3 inches long. Chiffonade: leafy herbs or greens stacked, rolled tight, and sliced across into thin ribbons.
Precision isn't decoration. Pieces of one size cook in the same time, so a pan of brunoise is done all at once, and a sauce built on it is smooth.

French cooking builds on two aromatic foundations. Mirepoix is onion, carrot, and celery in a 2:1:1 ratio by weight, diced to suit the cooking time: brunoise for a quick sauce, large dice for a long stock. Herbs come as a bouquet garni, a bundle of thyme, bay leaf, and parsley stems tied together so it can be lifted out, or as fines herbes, parsley, chives, tarragon, and chervil, chopped fine and added at the end.
Speed comes from repetition, not hurry. Keep the claw, let the blade do the work, and keep each cut the same before you try to make it faster.

quiz.q: What size is a brunoise?
A small dice is cut from which stick?
What's the mirepoix ratio by weight?
Why is a bouquet garni tied?
choices: So it can be lifted out

quiz.q: When do fines herbes go in?
quiz.explain: Delicate herbs lose flavor with long cooking.

quiz.q: Why cut to an exact size?
choices: Pieces of one size cook in the same time

sabbath.title: Prep every vegetable for a weekend meal
body: A weekend meal is easier to serve when every vegetable is cut beforehand. Done right, the day itself is only cooking.

Most firm vegetables keep 3 to 4 days cut: onions, carrots, celery, peppers, and squash, in sealed containers lined with paper towel. Tomatoes, cucumbers, potatoes, apples, and herbs are cut on the day, or held as noted: potatoes under cold water for up to a day, herbs whole in a damp towel.
steps: Choose the weekend menu and list every vegetable and its cut.
Group the list by what keeps and what doesn't.
Cut the keeping vegetables to the sizes the recipes need, each in its own lined container.
Label each with the recipe, the cut, and the date.
Write a short note of what's left to cut on the day, and how long it will take.
After the meal, note what worked and what you'd change.

quiz.q: Which keeps well cut for several days?
How do cut potatoes wait?
choices: Under cold water, up to a day

quiz.q: Why label each container with the recipe and cut?
choices: So the day's cooking is only cooking

drill.title: Weigh vs. measure; weigh the trim to find the yield
body: Today you'll see the difference between measuring and weighing with your own numbers, then find a real yield.
steps: Scoop 1 cup of flour three ways: scooped and packed, spooned and leveled, and sifted in. Weigh each and write it down.
Measure 1 cup of water and weigh it. It should be close to 8⅓ ounces.
Weigh a whole onion. Peel it, trim the root and top, and weigh it again. Work out the yield.
Do the same with a bell pepper: weigh, core and seed, weigh again.
Compare your yields with the Knowledge page's typical numbers.
Keep the trim for stock.

quiz.q: 1 cup of water weighs about:
quiz.explain: A cup of water weighs a little over 8 ounces.

quiz.q: Which flour cup weighs most?
A 10-ounce onion gives 9 ounces peeled. Yield?

knowledge.title: Why weight beats volume; trim loss and buying enough
body: A cup is a volume, and how much fits in it depends on how it's filled. A cup of flour can weigh anywhere from 4¼ to 5¼ ounces; a cup of chopped onion varies more. An ounce is an ounce.
That's why professional kitchens weigh. A scale gives the same result every time, in any hands, and it lets you scale a recipe by multiplication without converting cups and spoons.

Weight also tells you what you're really getting. Yield is the usable weight divided by the bought weight. Typical yields: onions about 90 percent after peeling; bell peppers 80 to 85; carrots 85 to 90; boneless steak trimmed 85 to 90; and meat loses another 20 to 30 percent of its trimmed weight in cooking.

To buy enough, work backward: the plated weight you need, divided by the yield. For 4 servings of 5 ounces of cooked steak (20 ounces) at a 75 percent cooking yield, you need about 27 ounces trimmed, and at 88 percent trim yield, about 30 ounces (1⅞ pounds) as bought.
Small amounts of salt, spices, and leaveners are still often given in spoons, because home scales aren't precise below about a tenth of an ounce.

quiz.q: Why weigh instead of using cups?
choices: An ounce is the same every time

quiz.q: What is yield?
You need 20 ounces cooked at a 75% cooking yield. How much trimmed meat?
Why are teaspoons still used for salt?
choices: Home scales aren't precise for tiny amounts

quiz.q: About what does steak lose in cooking?

sabbath.title: Weigh and portion ingredients ahead
body: Weighing and portioning ahead turns a recipe into a kit: open the containers and cook.
Dry ingredients can be weighed days ahead. Raw meat can be trimmed and portioned up to 2 days ahead in the fridge, or frozen; keep it sealed, on the bottom shelf, away from anything eaten raw.
steps: Pick a recipe for the weekend and convert its main ingredients to weights in ounces and pounds.
Weigh each dry ingredient into a labeled container or bag.
Trim and portion any meat, weigh each portion, and seal it. Wash your hands, board, and knife afterward.
Store the meat on the bottom shelf of the fridge, or freeze it.
Label everything with the recipe, the weight, and the date.
When you cook, note how much time it saved.

quiz.q: How long can trimmed raw meat wait in the fridge?
Where does raw meat go in the fridge?
quiz.explain: So nothing drips onto other food.

drill.title: Scale a recipe on paper, then check it against the app's amounts
body: Scale a recipe by hand, then check yourself against the app.
steps: Pick this week's enchiladas or chana masala.
Work out the factor to 12 servings.
On paper, multiply every ingredient, converting volumes to sensible amounts.
Mark which items you'd scale under the factor, and why.
Set the recipe's servings to 12 in the app and compare line by line.
Note every difference and decide whether yours or the app's is better for the dish.

quiz.q: How do you find the factor?
What do you do with a result like 2.25 eggs?
Which do you mark to scale under?

knowledge.title: Scaling factors, and what doesn't scale: salt, spice, time, pan size
body: The scaling factor is the servings you want divided by the servings written. From 4 to 12, it's 3. From 6 to 4, it's about 0.67. Multiply every ingredient by it, and round counted items sensibly.
Weights scale cleanly. Volumes do too, but convert awkward results: ⅓ cup × 3 is 1 cup; 1 teaspoon × 3 is 1 tablespoon; 3 tablespoons × 3 is ½ cup plus 1 tablespoon.

Some things don't scale in a straight line. Salt, spices, and chile heat build faster in a big batch: start at about three quarters of the full factor, then taste. Liquids that evaporate, like a simmering sauce, need less than the full factor, because a bigger pot loses less in proportion. Leaveners in baking are often scaled a little under.
Time doesn't multiply. A pot of soup three times the size takes longer to come to a boil, but simmers about the same. Baking time stays the same per pan, as long as the pans are the same size.
Pans don't stretch. A tripled recipe needs three pans of the original size, or one pan with three times the area, at the same depth. Check the oven fits them, and rotate them halfway.

quiz.q: What's the scaling factor from 6 to 4?
How should salt be scaled up?
choices: Under the full factor, then taste

quiz.q: A tripled cake in three pans bakes:
1 teaspoon × 3 is:
Why does a big batch of sauce need less extra liquid?
choices: A bigger pot loses less in proportion

sabbath.title: Scale a Sabbath recipe to the guest count
body: A Sabbath meal often has guests, so the family recipe has to fit the table. Scale it ahead, shop to the new amounts, and plan the pans before the day.
steps: Choose a recipe your family makes for Sabbath meals, and the number of guests.
Work out the factor and scale every ingredient by hand.
Adjust salt and spices under the factor, to taste on the day.
Plan the pans and the oven space, and any timing changes.
Write the shopping list from your scaled amounts.
Keep the scaled recipe with your notes for next time.

What should you plan besides amounts?

drill.title: Write a prep timeline and run it with a timer
body: Write a timeline for this week's mastery dish, then run it against a timer and see where it slips.
steps: Pick salade niçoise, bibimbap, or your own dish.
List each component with its active and passive time.
Choose a serving time and write each step as a clock time, working backward.
Check for collisions: hands, burners, and oven.
Cook to the timeline with a timer running, and note the actual time of each step.
Afterward, compare planned and actual times, and rewrite the timeline for next time.

quiz.q: What do you note while cooking?
choices: The actual time of each step

quiz.q: What's a collision?
choices: Two jobs needing the same hands or burner at once

quiz.q: When do you rewrite the timeline?

knowledge.title: Planning a meal backward from serving time
body: Every meal has a fixed point: the moment it's served. Plan from there backward.
List every component with its active time, hands busy, and its passive time, waiting. A roast might be 15 minutes active and 90 passive; a salad 15 active and nothing passive.
Place each component so it finishes at serving time, counting resting and holding: meat rests 10 minutes, rice holds covered for 20, and dressed greens wilt within minutes, so they go last.

Now check for collisions. Two jobs needing your hands at once, or two pans needing the same burner or the oven at different temperatures, must be moved. Passive time is when you do the active work of something else.
Add slack: 10 to 15 percent of the total, at the start. Write the plan as clock times, not durations, and keep it in view while you cook.

quiz.q: What's the fixed point of a meal plan?
What is passive time?
What goes last?
How much slack should you add?
How should the plan be written?

sabbath.title: Plan a Sabbath prep timeline
body: A Sabbath meal is cooked before the Sabbath begins and served without last-minute work. That makes the timeline run backward from sundown on Friday, with food held hot or served cold.
steps: Choose the Sabbath menu and note which dishes are served hot and which cold.
Mark sundown on Friday as your fixed point.
List every component, with its active and passive time and how it will be held.
Spread the work over Thursday and Friday so Friday afternoon isn't crowded.
Write the timeline as days and clock times, with slack before sundown.
After the meal, note what you'd move, and keep the plan.

quiz.q: What's the fixed point for a Sabbath meal?
Why spread the work over two days?
What do you note for each dish?
choices: Active time, passive time, and how it's held

drill.title: Make mayonnaise, break it, and rescue it
body: Make a mayonnaise, break it on purpose, and bring it back. Once you've rescued one, a broken sauce stops being a disaster. Use pasteurized eggs, and cook the yolk to 160°F first, as this week's recipes do.
steps: Whisk 1 pasteurized egg yolk with 1 teaspoon of lemon juice and 1 teaspoon of water in a heatproof bowl over barely simmering water until it thickens and probes 160°F. Wash your hands after separating the egg.
Off the heat, whisk for a minute to cool it, then add ½ teaspoon of mustard and a pinch of salt.
Measure ¾ cup of neutral oil. Whisk in the first quarter drop by drop, then the rest in a thin stream. Note when it turns thick and pale.
Take a third of the finished mayonnaise into a second bowl. Pour 3 tablespoons of oil in at once and whisk. Watch it break into a greasy, curdled pool.
Rescue it: in a clean bowl, whisk 1 teaspoon of mustard with 1 teaspoon of water. Whisk the broken mayonnaise in a teaspoon at a time until it's thick again.
Compare the two by look and taste, and write down what broke it and what saved it.
Keep the mayonnaise in a covered jar in the fridge and use it within 4 days, in this week's Caesar or ensaladilla.

quiz.q: What breaks a mayonnaise?
choices: Oil added faster than the emulsion can take it
quiz.explain: The droplets merge and the oil separates.

quiz.q: How do you rescue a broken mayonnaise?
choices: Whisk it slowly into a fresh emulsifier
quiz.explain: Mustard and water, or a fresh cooked yolk, then the broken sauce a little at a time.

quiz.q: How long does homemade mayonnaise keep in the fridge?

knowledge.title: Emulsions, and raw eggs: the USDA guideline and pasteurized eggs
body: An emulsion is one liquid dispersed through another as droplets: oil droplets in a water-based liquid in mayonnaise and vinaigrette, water droplets in fat in butter. The two phases don't mix, so an emulsion needs energy (whisking breaks the oil into droplets) and an emulsifier, a molecule with a water-loving end and a fat-loving end that coats each droplet and keeps it from merging with its neighbors.

Egg yolk is the strongest emulsifier in the kitchen. Its lecithin and proteins hold a mayonnaise stable for days, and one yolk can carry well over a cup of oil. Mustard is weaker but useful: it steadies a vinaigrette for an hour instead of a minute. Without an emulsifier, a vinaigrette is a temporary emulsion that separates as soon as you stop.

Three things break an emulsion: oil added faster than there are droplets to hold it, too much oil for the emulsifier (more than about 1½ cups to a yolk), and temperature, since a very cold or a warm sauce loses its grip. The fix is always the same: start a fresh emulsifier and whisk the broken sauce into it slowly.

Now the eggs. Salmonella Enteritidis can be inside an intact, clean egg, passed from the hen before the shell forms, so washing doesn't remove it. The USDA and FDA advise against eating raw or undercooked eggs and say to cook egg dishes to 160°F. The risk is highest for young children, older adults, pregnant women, and anyone with a weakened immune system.

For recipes that use eggs raw, the USDA's answer is pasteurized eggs: in-shell eggs heated in a water bath just enough to kill Salmonella without cooking them, or pasteurized liquid egg products. Store-bought mayonnaise is made with pasteurized eggs and enough acid to be shelf-stable until opened.

This app keeps one standard for every egg: 160°F. So the Level 4 recipes use pasteurized eggs and still cook the yolks to 160°F with the lemon juice before the oil goes in. Cooked this way, the yolk keeps its emulsifying power, and the sauce is safe for every guest at the table.
Homemade mayonnaise and egg-based dressings have no preservatives. Keep them covered in the fridge at 40°F or below and use them within 4 days.

quiz.q: What does an emulsifier do?
choices: Coats droplets so they don't merge
quiz.explain: One end holds water, the other fat.

quiz.q: Why doesn't washing make a raw egg safe?
choices: Salmonella can be inside an intact egg
quiz.explain: It's passed from the hen before the shell forms.

quiz.q: To what temperature does the USDA say to cook egg dishes?
quiz.explain: The app uses this for every egg.

quiz.q: What is a pasteurized in-shell egg?
choices: Heated just enough to kill Salmonella without cooking
An egg from a special breed
quiz.explain: The USDA's answer for raw-egg recipes.

quiz.q: A mayonnaise broke. What's the fix?
choices: Whisk it slowly into a fresh emulsifier
quiz.explain: Mustard and water, or a new cooked yolk.

quiz.q: How long does homemade mayonnaise keep?

sabbath.title: Make a dressing ahead
body: A dressing made ahead turns a week of salads, wraps, and grain bowls into assembly. Most keep well, but not equally.

A plain vinaigrette of oil, vinegar, salt, and mustard keeps up to 2 weeks in the fridge. Add fresh garlic, shallot, or herbs and the clock shortens to about 4 days: fresh garlic held in oil is a botulism risk if it's left out, so it stays cold and gets used soon. An egg- or dairy-based dressing, like this week's Caesar or a yogurt dressing, keeps 3 to 4 days.
Olive oil firms up in the fridge. Take the jar out 15 minutes before you need it, or run it under warm water, and shake it hard; it re-emulsifies in seconds.
steps: Plan four meals this week that use a dressing.
Make a double batch of a vinaigrette, with mustard, and a single batch of a creamy dressing: this week's Caesar or a yogurt dressing.
Jar each one, and label it with the name, the date made, and the use-by date from the guide above.
Store them on a fridge shelf, not the door, where the temperature swings.
Use them through the week, and note which held up and which didn't.

quiz.q: How long does a vinaigrette with fresh garlic keep?
quiz.explain: Fresh garlic in oil is a botulism risk.

quiz.q: Why store dressings on a shelf, not the door?
The olive oil vinaigrette is solid from the fridge. What do you do?
choices: Let it warm 15 minutes and shake it

drill.title: Hold a cold platter below 41°F; the 2-hour rule
body: Run a cold-holding test before you hold food for guests. You'll set out two identical plates, one on ice and one not, and log both for 2 hours.
steps: Chill two plates and a sheet pan of ice packs or frozen water for 30 minutes.
Cut two equal sets of perishable food from the fridge: cheese cubes, cut tomato, and a scoop of a dip.
Set one plate on the ice tray and one on the counter. Probe the cheese on each and log the time and temperature.
Probe both every 30 minutes for 2 hours. Note the room temperature too.
Graph or table your readings. When did the counter plate pass 41°F? Did the iced plate ever?
Discard the counter plate's food at 2 hours. Refrigerate the iced plate's food only if every reading was 41°F or below.

quiz.q: What's the cold-holding limit?
What happens to food left off ice for 2 hours?
choices: It goes back in the fridge

quiz.q: How often do you probe a cold platter?

knowledge.title: Food safety for a cold buffet
body: A buffet is the riskiest way to serve food: it sits out, many hands reach in, and nobody is watching the clock. Food safety codes call the risky foods TCS, time/temperature control for safety: anything moist and protein-rich or cut, where bacteria can grow. On a cold table that means sliced meats, cheeses, dips like hummus and labneh, cut tomatoes and melons, leafy greens, cooked grains and beans, and anything with mayonnaise.

Cold holding has a number: 41°F or below, from the FDA Food Code that restaurants follow (your home fridge should run at 40°F or below). There are two ways to control it. Temperature: on ice, probed and logged, with nothing above 41°F. Or time: off ice, out for no more than 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90°F, then discarded, not returned to the fridge.

Cooked food headed for a cold table has to get cold fast. The rule is two-stage cooling: from 135°F to 70°F within 2 hours, then to 41°F within the next 4. Big, deep containers can't do it; the middle stays warm for hours. Spread food shallow, under 2 inches, and leave it uncovered until it's cool.

Listeria is the cold table's special concern. It grows even at fridge temperature and is found in deli meats and soft cheeses. It's most dangerous during pregnancy and for older adults, which is one more reason cold food stays cold and isn't held for days.

Good buffet practice: small platters, refilled from the fridge on clean plates, never topped up with fresh food on top of old; a separate serving utensil for every dish; bread off the ice and away from the dips; and a written log of times and temperatures. At the end, food that held at 41°F on ice can be refrigerated; anything else is thrown away.
This is a professional's standard, and it's what lets you feed a crowd without making anyone sick.

quiz.q: What's the two-stage cooling rule?
choices: 135°F to 70°F in 2 hours, then to 41°F in 4

sabbath.title: Hospitality: Abraham's meal for his guests (Genesis 18:1–8; Hebrews 13:2)
body: Abraham was sitting at the door of his tent in the heat of the day when he saw three men standing nearby. He ran to meet them, bowed, and begged them to stay: "Let a little water be brought, and wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree, while I bring a morsel of bread" (Genesis 18:4–5).

The "morsel" was a feast. Abraham hurried to Sarah, who made cakes from three seahs of fine flour, enough for a crowd. He ran to the herd himself, chose a calf, "tender and good," and a young man hurried to prepare it. He set it before them with curds and milk, and stood by them under the tree while they ate (Genesis 18:6–8). The guests were the LORD and two angels, though Abraham welcomed them before he knew it.

The New Testament remembers this scene: "Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for thereby some have entertained angels unawares" (Hebrews 13:2). Paul tells believers to "seek to show hospitality" (Romans 12:13), and Peter adds, "without grumbling" (1 Peter 4:9).

Notice what Abraham did: he ran, he offered his best rather than his leftovers, he served the guests himself, and he stayed with them while they ate. Hospitality was a matter of the heart, and also of planning and work.
steps: Read Genesis 18:1–8 and Hebrews 13:1–2.
Read Romans 12:13 and 1 Peter 4:9.
Answer in writing: list every action Abraham took, from seeing the guests to standing by them. What does each show?
Answer in writing: what's the difference between hosting to impress and hosting as Abraham did?
With your family, plan a meal for a guest this month: someone new, alone, or in need. Write the menu from your Unit 1 and 2 recipes, the shopping list, and the budget.
If you can, host it, and use this week's cold-holding skills for anything set out.

drill.title: Break a chicken into 8 pieces; save the back for stock
body: A whole chicken breaks into eight serving pieces with nothing but a sharp chef's knife and a feel for the joints. Do it once slowly, naming each joint as you find it, then again for time. Use the pieces in this week's recipe.
steps: Set up: the raw-meat board on a damp towel, a sharp chef's knife, a sheet pan for the pieces, a bag for the back, and hot, soapy water ready. Don't rinse the bird.

Legs: lay the chicken breast up. Pull a leg away from the body, slice through the skin between leg and breast, then bend the leg back until the hip joint pops out. Cut through the joint, scooping the chicken oyster (the round pocket of meat on the back) out with the thigh. Repeat.
Split each leg: skin side down, find the line of fat over the knee joint, and cut straight down through it into drumstick and thigh.
Wings: pull each wing out, find the shoulder joint by wiggling it, and cut through.
Back: stand the bird on its neck end and cut down through the ribs on both sides, separating the breast from the back.
Breast: lay it skin side up and cut through the breastbone, just off center, into two halves. For four breast pieces, halve each across.
Line up the 8 pieces and the back. Weigh the pieces and the back separately, and note both.
Bag and freeze the back (Beyond the Recipe). Wash the knife, board, and pan, wipe the counter and the faucet, and wash your hands.
Next time, time yourself. A cook who knows the joints takes under 5 minutes.

quiz.q: How do you find where to cut a leg off?
choices: Bend it back until the hip joint pops, then cut through the joint

quiz.q: What is the chicken oyster?
choices: A round pocket of meat on the back, kept with the thigh
quiz.explain: It's the best bite on the bird.

quiz.q: What marks the knee joint from the outside?
choices: A line of fat across the leg
quiz.explain: Cut straight down through the fat line.

knowledge.title: Yield and cost: a whole bird vs. parts
body: A whole chicken almost always costs less per pound than the same chicken sold in parts, because the store charges for the butchering. But some of a whole bird's weight is back, neck, and bone you won't serve. The question is what you pay per pound of what you actually eat.

Yield is the weight you use divided by the weight you bought. A 4-pound chicken usually gives about 2⅞ pounds of serving pieces (breasts, thighs, drumsticks, wings) and 1⅛ pounds of back, neck, and trim. That's a yield of about 72 percent.

Here's the math with sample prices; your store's will differ. A whole chicken at $1.50 a pound, 4 pounds, costs $6.00. Divided by the 2⅞ pounds of pieces, that's $2.09 a pound of serving pieces. Bought separately, bone-in thighs might be $2.00 a pound and breasts $4.00, a mix averaging around $2.95. The whole bird wins, and the back becomes free stock.
The break-even point is the parts price at which the whole bird stops saving money: whole-bird price divided by yield. If parts ever cost less than that, buy parts.
What the math leaves out: your time (about 5 minutes once you're practiced), freezer space, and whether your family eats every part. A whole bird pays only if nothing is wasted.
steps: Find today's prices at your store for a whole chicken, bone-in thighs, drumsticks, wings, and breasts.
Use your weights from the drill to work out your bird's yield and its cost per pound of serving pieces.
Work out the break-even parts price, and compare it with the store's.
Write two sentences: which was cheaper this week, and when you'd choose the other.

quiz.q: What is yield?
choices: The weight you use divided by the weight you bought

quiz.q: A 5-pound bird gives 3.6 pounds of pieces. What's the yield?
A whole bird costs $1.50 a pound with a 72% yield. What's the break-even parts price?
What does the yield math leave out?
choices: Your time, freezer space, and waste
quiz.explain: A bird only pays if every part is used.

sabbath.title: Freeze the back and wings for stock
body: The back, neck, and wing tips from a whole chicken are the start of a good stock: mostly bone and connective tissue, which is what gives stock its body. Saved in the freezer until there's enough, they cost nothing extra.
steps: Bag the back and wing tips from this week's chicken in a freezer bag. Press out the air.
Label the bag with the date and "chicken backs for stock." Keep a running count on the label as you add more.
Freeze it flat, so it stacks and thaws quickly. Use it within 3 months.
When you have the backs of 2 or 3 chickens (about 3 pounds), they're enough for about 3 quarts of stock: cover with cold water, add onion, carrot, celery, bay, and peppercorns, and simmer 3 hours.
Wash your hands and everything the raw chicken touched.

quiz.q: Why are backs good for stock?
choices: They're mostly bone and connective tissue, which give stock its body

quiz.q: How long do frozen backs keep?
Why freeze the bag flat?

drill.title: Trim silverskin; score duck skin
body: Two trims a restaurant prep cook does every day: taking silverskin off beef, and scoring duck skin so its fat renders. Do the one for the dish you're cooking this week on its own meat. For the other, watch a short video and practice the knife work on a vegetable, so you don't buy a second cut.
steps: If you're cooking the flank steak: lay it on the raw-meat board and find the thin, shiny membrane on its surface.
Slide the tip of a sharp, flexible knife under one end of it. Grip the freed tab with a paper towel.

Angle the blade slightly up, toward the membrane, and saw gently along under it while pulling the tab back. Take it off in strips, losing as little meat as you can. Weigh the trim and note it as a percentage of the steak.

If you're cooking the duck: lay a breast skin side up. With the tip of the knife, cut lines ⅜ inch apart diagonally across the skin, through the fat but not into the meat. Turn it and cut the other way, for diamonds. No red meat should show; if it does, cut shallower.
For the trim you aren't doing, watch a short video of it (search "remove silverskin from steak" or "score duck breast").

Then practice that motion on a vegetable: score a crosshatch through the skin of a halved eggplant or zucchini without cutting into the flesh, or slide the knife just under the peel of a cucumber, blade angled up, taking off a thin strip.
Refrigerate the meat for this week's recipe, use the vegetable in a stir-fry or salad, and wash your hands, the knife, and the board.

quiz.q: Which way does the blade angle when you remove silverskin?
quiz.explain: So you lose as little meat as possible.

quiz.q: How deep do you score duck skin?
choices: Through the skin and fat, not into the meat
Only the surface of the skin

quiz.q: Why remove silverskin?
choices: It tightens and turns rubbery when cooked

knowledge.title: Primal cuts and the method each suits
body: A beef carcass is first cut into large sections called primals, and each primal into the cuts you buy. Knowing which primal a cut comes from tells you how hard that muscle worked, and so how to cook it.

Chuck (the shoulder) works constantly: flavorful, full of connective tissue, and best braised or stewed (pot roast, stew meat, ground chuck). Rib and short loin (along the upper back) barely work: tender, marbled cuts for dry, fast heat (ribeye, strip, tenderloin). Sirloin, behind them, is a little firmer and still good seared or grilled. Round (the hind leg) is lean and tough unless sliced thin or braised. Brisket and plate (the chest and belly) are fatty and tough, made for long, slow cooking. Flank, below the loin, is lean and fibrous, with lots of flavor: seared hot, sliced thin across the grain.

The rule: muscles that move a lot are tough and suited to moist, slow heat (braising, stewing); muscles that move little are tender and suited to dry, fast heat (searing, grilling, roasting). Lamb follows the same map: shoulder and shank for braising, rack and loin for roasting.

Poultry follows it too. Legs work and are dark, rich, and forgiving; breasts are lean and dry quickly. Duck breast is darker than chicken breast because ducks fly: it's a working muscle, rich and red, and it slices like a steak.
steps: Draw a simple outline of a steer and divide it into the primals on this page: chuck, rib, short loin, sirloin, round, brisket, plate, flank.
On each, write one cut and one cooking method.
At a store or butcher, find three beef cuts. Write down each primal, its price per pound, and how you'd cook it.

quiz.q: Which primal is best for braising?
Why is flank sliced thin across the grain?
choices: It's lean and fibrous; short fibers are tender

quiz.q: Why is duck breast darker than chicken breast?
choices: Ducks fly, so the breast is a working muscle

quiz.q: Which method suits a tender cut like ribeye?
choices: Dry, fast heat: searing or grilling

sabbath.title: Clean birds: duck, goose, quail, and the birds Leviticus names (Leviticus 11:13–19)
body: Leviticus 11:13–19 lists the birds Israel was not to eat: the eagle, the vultures, the kite and falcon, every raven, the ostrich, the nighthawk and sea gull, the hawk, the owls, the cormorant, the stork, the heron, the hoopoe, and the bat. Most hunt or eat what's already dead. Deuteronomy 14:11–20 repeats the list and adds, "All clean winged things you may eat."

Every bird not on the list is clean. That includes the domestic birds raised for food (chicken, turkey, duck, goose) and many game birds: quail, pheasant, partridge, grouse, guinea fowl, and pigeon and dove. Scripture shows clean birds in use: turtledoves and pigeons as offerings (Leviticus 1:14; 12:8), and quail sent to Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 16:13).
This week's duck and week 10's quail are both clean. Duck and goose are richer than chicken, with dark breast meat and a thick layer of fat under the skin, which is why they're scored and rendered.
steps: Read Leviticus 11:13–19 and Deuteronomy 14:11–20.
Sort these into clean and unclean using the passages: duck, goose, heron, quail, ostrich, pheasant, raven, turkey.
Look up the hoopoe and the cormorant. Write one sentence on what each eats.
Find duck, quail, or another game bird at a store or online. Write down the price per pound and compare it with chicken.

quiz.q: How does Leviticus 11 identify unclean birds?
Which of these is clean?
What does Deuteronomy 14:20 say?
choices: "All clean winged things you may eat"
quiz.explain: Every bird not listed is clean.

drill.title: Skin and portion a side of salmon; pull the pin bones
body: A whole side of salmon costs less per pound than portions, and portioning it yourself is quick once you've done it. If your family is cooking the teriyaki salmon side, this drill is its first steps. If you're cooking the veracruzana, don't buy a side for it: watch a fishmonger do it on video, then practice on one skin-on fillet.
steps: Cooking the veracruzana instead? Watch a short video of a side of salmon being skinned and portioned (search "how to portion a side of salmon"), then do the steps below on one skin-on salmon fillet, and cook it any way you like this week.
Lay the side skin down on the raw-meat board with the head end to your left (to your right if you're left-handed).
Run your fingertips along the thick half, from the head end toward the tail. Pull each pin bone with tweezers toward the head, at the angle it lies. Count them; a side usually has 25 to 35.
Turn the side so the tail points toward you. Cut down through the flesh to the skin about ¾ inch from the tail end.
Grip the tail flap of skin with a paper towel. Hold the knife nearly flat against the skin, and pull the skin toward you in small side-to-side movements while the knife stays almost still.
Trim off the thin belly fat along the bottom edge and any brown flesh on the skinned side.
Portion by weight: about 5 ounces each. Cut the thick head end into narrower pieces and the tail into wider ones, folding the thinnest tail under.
Weigh the trim and the skin. Note the yield.
Wash the knife, tweezers, board, and your hands with hot, soapy water.

quiz.q: How do you hold the knife when skinning?
choices: Nearly flat against the skin, almost still, while you pull the skin

quiz.q: How do you portion a side evenly?
choices: By weight, narrower at the thick end and wider at the tail

quiz.q: About how many pin bones does a side of salmon have?
quiz.explain: They run along the thick half.

knowledge.title: Buying fish: wild and farmed, labels, questions for the fish counter
body: Every fish sold at a U.S. counter must be labeled with its name, where it came from, and whether it was wild-caught or farm-raised. Those three things, plus a few questions, tell you most of what you need.

Name. On a fillet or steak you can't see the scales, so the name is how you know a fish is clean (fins and scales, Leviticus 11:9). Watch for vague names. "Snapper" sold in some places covers several kinds; "red snapper" is one species. Fish that are commonly substituted include snapper, grouper, and cod. If a name is vague or the price is far below other stores, ask.

Wild or farmed. Wild salmon is leaner, deeper in color, and seasonal; farmed salmon is fattier, milder, and steady in price and supply. Both are clean. Farmed fish vary with how they're raised; certification labels from independent groups tell you a farm meets set standards for feed, crowding, and the water around it.

Fresh, frozen, and "previously frozen." Fish frozen at sea within hours of the catch is often better than "fresh" fish that's been on ice for a week. "Previously frozen" at the counter means it was thawed for display: cook it within a day and don't refreeze it.
Questions for the fish counter: What is it, exactly? Where's it from? When did it come in? Was it frozen? Can I smell it? Will you scale and gut it, or skin it?
steps: At a fish counter, read the labels on four fish. Write down each one's name, origin, and wild or farmed.
Ask two of the questions on this page, and write down the answers.
Compare the price per pound of a side of salmon with salmon portions. Using your drill yield, work out the real cost of the side per pound of portions.

quiz.q: What three things must a U.S. fish label show?
choices: Its name, where it's from, and wild or farmed

quiz.q: What does "previously frozen" mean at the counter?
choices: It was thawed for display: cook within a day, don't refreeze
quiz.explain: Thawed fish has a short clock.

quiz.q: Why does the fish's name matter most?
choices: Without the skin, it's how you know the fish has fins and scales
It tells you how to cook it

quiz.q: A label says "snapper." What do you do?
choices: Ask which kind, and whether it's red snapper
quiz.explain: Snapper is a name some stores use loosely.

sabbath.title: Fins and scales, and the fishermen Jesus called (Leviticus 11:9–12; Luke 5:1–11)
body: "These you may eat, of all that are in the waters. Everything in the waters that has fins and scales, whether in the seas or in the rivers, you may eat" (Leviticus 11:9). The rule is repeated in Deuteronomy 14:9–10.

In Luke 5:1–11, Jesus borrows Simon Peter's boat to teach the crowd from the water. Afterward He tells Peter to put out into deep water and let down the nets. Peter answers, "Master, we toiled all night and took nothing! But at your word I will let down the nets" (Luke 5:5). The catch is so large the nets begin to break and two boats nearly sink.
Peter falls at Jesus' knees. Jesus tells him, "Do not be afraid; from now on you will be catching men" (Luke 5:10). They brought their boats to land, left everything, and followed Him (Luke 5:11).
The disciples' trade was the fish of the Sea of Galilee, sold in the markets and salted for the cities, and the Gospels return to those boats and nets again and again.
steps: Read Leviticus 11:9–12 and Luke 5:1–11.
Answer in writing: what did Peter's answer in Luke 5:5 show about him?
Answer in writing: what did the fishermen leave behind in Luke 5:11, and what would that have meant for their families' living?
Find two more Gospel passages where Jesus meets His disciples at their boats or eats fish with them (start with Mark 1:16–20 and John 21).

quiz.q: What did Peter say when Jesus told him to let down the nets?
choices: "At your word I will let down the nets"

quiz.q: What happened to the nets?
choices: They began to break from the catch

quiz.q: What two things must a water animal have to be clean?

drill.title: Spatchcock a bird
body: Spatchcocking, cutting out the backbone and pressing a bird flat, makes a whole bird roast evenly and fast. Use this week's birds, so nothing extra is needed: spatchcock the quail for the Explore dish, or, for chicken two ways, spatchcock the chicken first, then break it down from flat. The backbone goes into the stock either way.
steps: Set up the raw-meat station. Lay the bird breast side down, neck end toward you. Don't rinse it.
With kitchen shears, cut along one side of the backbone from tail to neck, cutting through the rib bones.
Cut along the other side and lift the backbone out. Bag it for stock.
Open the bird like a book. Nick the white cartilage at the top of the breastbone with the knife tip.
Turn it skin side up, legs pointing out. Press hard on the breastbone with the heel of your hand until it cracks and the bird lies flat.
Tuck the wing tips behind the breast. If you're cooking chicken two ways, go straight on to breaking it down: the legs, wings, and breasts come off a flat bird easily.
A flat 4-pound chicken would roast at 450°F in about 45 minutes, to 165°F in the thickest part of the breast and thigh; flat quail take about 14 minutes.
Wash the shears, board, and your hands with hot, soapy water, and wipe the counter.

quiz.q: What do you cut out to spatchcock a bird?
Why spatchcock?
choices: The bird roasts evenly and faster

quiz.q: What tool cuts through the ribs most easily?

knowledge.title: Cost per serving, from the receipt
body: Cost per serving is what restaurants live by and what most home cooks never calculate. It's simple: the total cost of what a dish used, divided by the servings it made.

Start with the receipt. For each ingredient, work out what fraction of the package the recipe used: half a bag of noodles, the whole of a 4-pound chicken, a tenth of a jar of thyme. Multiply each package price by that fraction and add them up. Spices and oil are small but count; round them to the nearest few cents.
Divide by servings. If this week's chicken two ways used $18.60 of ingredients and made 6 servings of soup and 6 of breast, that's $1.55 per serving; as 6 dinners of both together, $3.10.

Compare. A dish's cost per serving is useful next to something: the same dish from store-bought parts and stock, a restaurant's price, or your family's grocery budget per meal. What a whole bird saves shows up here: the stock you didn't buy, the parts you didn't pay a butcher for.
Food cost percentage, the restaurant measure, is the ingredient cost divided by the menu price. Many restaurants aim for about 28 to 35 percent; the rest pays for labor, rent, and everything else.
steps: Using this week's receipt, list every ingredient in your mastery dish, its package price, and the fraction you used.
Add up the cost and divide by servings. Show your math.
Price the same meal made from store-bought parts and boxed stock, and from a restaurant. Write a short paragraph comparing the three.
Write down one change that would lower the cost per serving without changing the dish much.

quiz.q: How do you work out cost per serving?
choices: Total ingredient cost divided by servings
Price of the most expensive ingredient
Total grocery bill divided by days

quiz.q: A $4.00 jar of thyme; you used a tenth. What do you count?
A dish costs $3.00 to make and sells for $10.00. What's the food cost percentage?
Why does a whole bird lower cost per serving?
choices: You don't pay for butchering, and the back becomes stock

sabbath.title: Manna and quail (Exodus 16:13; Numbers 11:31–32)
body: In the wilderness, Israel complained of hunger, and God answered: "At twilight you shall eat meat, and in the morning you shall be filled with bread" (Exodus 16:12). "In the evening quail came up and covered the camp, and in the morning dew lay around the camp" (Exodus 16:13), and when the dew lifted, there was manna.

The manna came with instructions: gather what each person needs for the day; on the sixth day, gather twice as much (Exodus 16:16–26). Some gathered extra on other days, and it spoiled (Exodus 16:20). The provision was daily, and it was enough.

Numbers 11 tells of a later time, when the people grew tired of manna and craved meat. God sent quail again, in huge numbers (Numbers 11:31–32), but the people gathered greedily, and the story ends in judgment (Numbers 11:33–34). The same food was a gift in one story and a lesson in the other; the difference was the people's hearts.
Quail are clean birds (Deuteronomy 14:11), and this week's Explore dish cooks them.
steps: Read Exodus 16:1–21 and Numbers 11:4–6, 18–20, 31–34.
Answer in writing: how were the two quail stories alike, and how were they different?
Answer in writing: what did the manna instructions teach about trusting God for daily food?
Look at your family's grocery spending for one week. Write one way your family could waste less, as Israel was told to gather only what it needed.

quiz.q: What did God send Israel at twilight in Exodus 16?
What happened to extra manna gathered on an ordinary day?
In Numbers 11, what was wrong when quail came again?
choices: The people craved and gathered greedily

drill.title: Make a tangzhong; cold-retard a dough overnight
body: Two techniques from this week, practiced on their own: a tangzhong cooked by temperature, and a dough retarded overnight. Use the flour, milk, and yeast this week's recipe already buys.
steps: Whisk 1 tablespoon of flour into 3 tablespoons of milk in a small saucepan. Cook over low heat, whisking, with the thermometer in it.
Note what it looks like at 120°F, 140°F, and 149°F. Take it off at 149°F. When did it thicken?

Cooking the milk bread? This is its first step; keep going with the recipe. Cooking the babka? Stir the paste into a small test dough instead: ½ cup flour, 2 tablespoons warm milk, ¼ teaspoon yeast, a pinch each of sugar and salt.
Knead the test dough 5 minutes and split it in two balls.
Leave one ball covered at room temperature. Wrap the other and put it in the fridge overnight.
Next day, let the cold ball warm 1 hour, then bake both on a sheet pan at 375°F until golden.
Taste them side by side. Write down the difference in flavor, crust color, and crumb.

quiz.q: At what temperature does tangzhong thicken?
What did the retarded ball probably taste like?
choices: Deeper, a little tangy, and browner

quiz.q: Why let cold dough warm before baking?
choices: So the yeast wakes up and it bakes evenly

knowledge.title: Lean vs. enriched doughs; what cold fermentation adds
body: A lean dough is flour, water, yeast, and salt, maybe a little oil: baguettes, pita, pizza. An enriched dough adds fat, sugar, eggs, or milk: challah, brioche, babka, milk bread. The additions change everything about how the dough behaves.

Fat coats gluten strands and shortens them, so enriched breads are soft and tender rather than chewy. Sugar pulls water away from the yeast and feeds it at the same time; past about 10% of the flour's weight, it slows fermentation, which is why rich doughs rise slowly and sometimes use extra yeast. Eggs add protein that sets in the oven and lecithin that softens the crumb. Milk sugars and proteins brown the crust early, so enriched loaves are judged by 190°F, not color.

Cold fermentation, or retarding, means slowing a dough in the fridge for 8 to 72 hours. The yeast nearly stops, but the dough's enzymes keep breaking starch into sugars and proteins into flavor compounds, and bacteria make small amounts of acid. The bread tastes deeper and more complex, browns better, and keeps longer. For a rich dough there's a practical gain too: cold butter makes a soft dough firm enough to roll and shape cleanly.

Tangzhong, from Japan and China, works on a different lever: pre-cooking a little of the flour in liquid swells its starch so it holds several times its weight in water. The dough can carry more water without being sticky, and the bread stays soft for days.

Bakers describe doughs by percentages of the flour's weight, called baker's percentages: flour is always 100%. A lean dough might be 65% water and 2% salt; a babka is closer to 25% butter and 20% sugar. It's how a professional compares recipes at a glance.

This week's Explore dish is Japanese. Bread came to Japan from the West in the late 1800s, and Japanese bakeries made it their own: soft, slightly sweet milk breads, filled buns, and curry bread. Shokupan, the milk loaf, is sold by the loaf in every neighborhood bakery and toasted thick for breakfast.
steps: Take this week's recipe. Weigh or convert its flour, liquid, fat, and sugar to ounces.
Work out each as a baker's percentage of the flour. Write them in a table.
Do the same for the sandwich loaf or challah, if you've baked one, and compare. Which is richer?
Answer in writing: what two things does a night in the fridge do for a rich dough?

quiz.q: What makes a dough "enriched"?
choices: Added fat, sugar, eggs, or milk
quiz.explain: A lean dough is flour, water, yeast, and salt.

quiz.q: Why do rich doughs rise slowly?
choices: Fat coats the gluten and sugar pulls water from the yeast
quiz.explain: Some recipes add extra yeast to make up for it.

quiz.q: What does cold fermentation add?
choices: Deeper flavor, better browning, and a firmer dough to shape
quiz.explain: Enzymes keep working in the cold.

quiz.q: In baker's percentages, the flour is always…
quiz.explain: Everything else is measured against it.

quiz.q: What does tangzhong do?
choices: Swells starch so the dough holds more water and stays soft
quiz.explain: The bread keeps soft for days.

sabbath.title: Bread of the Presence (Leviticus 24:5–9)
body: In the tabernacle, God commanded twelve loaves of fine flour to be set out on a gold table before Him, in two rows of six, with pure frankincense beside them. Every Sabbath they were replaced with fresh bread, "a covenant forever," and the old loaves were eaten by Aaron and his sons in a holy place (Leviticus 24:5–9).
The loaves are called the bread of the Presence (Exodus 25:30), set "before the LORD regularly." Twelve loaves stood for the twelve tribes of Israel, kept always before God.

The bread comes back in the life of David. Fleeing Saul and hungry, David asked the priest Ahimelech for bread, and the only bread there was the holy bread just removed from the table. The priest gave it to him (1 Samuel 21:1–6). Jesus pointed to this story when the Pharisees accused His disciples of breaking the Sabbath by picking grain (Matthew 12:1–8), and said, "something greater than the temple is here."
steps: Read Leviticus 24:5–9 and Exodus 25:23–30.
Read 1 Samuel 21:1–6 and Matthew 12:1–8.
Each loaf used two-tenths of an ephah of flour, about 4 quarts. Work out roughly how many pounds of flour the twelve loaves took each week (a quart of flour weighs about 1¼ pounds).
Answer in writing: what did it mean that the bread was set out "regularly" and replaced every Sabbath?
Answer in writing: why do you think Jesus used David's story to answer the Pharisees?

quiz.q: How many loaves were set on the table?
choices: Twelve, in two rows of six

quiz.q: How often were they replaced?
Who ate the holy bread when fleeing Saul?
Where did Jesus refer to that story?
quiz.explain: When His disciples picked grain on the Sabbath.

drill.title: Lamination folds
body: Lamination is the skill this week: folding butter into dough so it stays in layers. You'll practice the folds on this week's rough puff and count what you make. If you're cooking the pot pie, the dough is its top crust; if the borekas, their pastry.
steps: Make this week's rough-puff dough up to the first roll. Weigh the dough and note the weight.
Roll it to a rectangle about 6 by 15 inches, the short side toward you. Measure it.
Brush off the flour. Fold the bottom third up and the top third down, like a letter. That's one fold.
Turn it a quarter turn so the open edge faces you. Roll and fold again.
Wrap and chill 15 minutes. Feel the dough before and after. What changed?
Do two more folds. Count the layers of butter: each fold triples them.
When you bake it, cut through one piece and look at the side. Can you count layers?

quiz.q: What is one letter fold?
choices: Folding the dough in thirds, like a letter

quiz.q: After two folds, what do you do?
quiz.explain: The butter firms and the gluten relaxes.

quiz.q: How many butter layers after four folds?

knowledge.title: Fats: butter vs. shortening; reading pastry labels
body: Pastry is mostly flour and fat, and the fat decides the result. Butter is about 80% fat and 16% water, and it melts at body temperature. The water turns to steam in the oven and lifts layers; the milk solids brown and taste rich. Its weakness is a narrow working range: too cold and it shatters, a few degrees too warm and it smears.

Vegetable shortening is 100% fat with no water. It stays solid over a wider range of temperatures, so it's easier to work and makes a tender, flaky crust, but with less flavor and less lift from steam. Many bakers use a mix. Oil makes a crumbly, mealy crust that doesn't flake.

In rough puff and puff pastry, the fat must stay in sheets between layers of dough. That needs butter cold enough to roll without smearing, chilling between folds, and a hot oven so the water in the butter turns to steam before the butter melts out.

Fats are where pastry hides ingredients this app keeps out. Store-bought pie crusts, puff pastry, phyllo, empanada discs, and some shortening blends can be made with the fats in the Watch for box. Butter, pure vegetable shortening, and oil are fine. Ingredient lists change, so read them each time, and check "shortening" on a label to see what it's made from.

This week's Explore dish is Turkish. Turkish home baking is built on layered doughs: yufka and phyllo sheets brushed with butter for börek, and rough or full puff for bakery borekas. The fillings stay simple: white cheese like feta, spinach, potato, or spiced meat, with dill, parsley, and black pepper.
steps: Read the ingredient lists on a box of store-bought pie crust, a box of puff pastry, and a can of shortening, online or at the store.
For each, write down the fat or fats it uses and whether your family can use it.
Work out the cost per ounce of store-bought puff pastry and of the butter and flour in this week's rough puff.

watch.name: Lard
watch.hides: Fat from pigs. In some store-bought pie crusts, puff pastry, empanada discs, and shortening blends.

watch.name: Suet and beef tallow
watch.hides: The hard fat of cattle and sheep, which Leviticus 3:17 and 7:23 forbid. In some pastry, mincemeat, and shortening blends.

quiz.q: What does butter have that shortening doesn't?
choices: About 16% water, which steams into layers, and milk solids for flavor

quiz.q: Why is shortening easier to work?
choices: It stays solid over a wider range of temperatures
quiz.explain: Butter has a narrow working range.

quiz.q: Why does rough puff need a hot oven?
choices: So the butter's water steams before the butter melts out

quiz.q: A label says only "shortening." What do you do?
choices: Check what the shortening is made from
quiz.explain: Some blends include fats on the Watch for list.

sabbath.title: Freeze unbaked borekas or a pot pie
body: Laminated pastry is made for the freezer. Shaped but unbaked, borekas and a pot pie's rough-puff lid go straight from the freezer to the oven, and the frozen butter makes them puff even better. A dinner that took an afternoon becomes a dinner that takes the baking time.
steps: Shape a batch of borekas, or a second pot-pie lid, and don't egg-wash them.
Borekas: freeze them on a lined sheet pan, not touching, until hard, about 2 hours. Move them to a freezer bag.
Pot pie: cool the filling completely, cover it in a foil pan or a freezer-safe dish, and lay the rough-puff lid over it. Wrap it in plastic, then foil.
Label each with the dish, the oven temperature, and the date. They keep 3 months.
To bake, don't thaw. Egg-wash, cut vents in the pie, and bake at the recipe's temperature: borekas about 10 minutes longer, a pot pie 25 to 35 minutes longer, with foil over the top once it browns.
Check the filling: 165°F for the pot pie, 160°F for the borekas.

quiz.q: Why freeze borekas on a pan first?
choices: So they freeze separately and don't stick

quiz.q: Why must the pot pie filling be cold before the lid goes on?
choices: Warm filling melts the butter layers

quiz.q: What temperature does a frozen pot pie's filling need to reach?
quiz.explain: The crust browns long before the middle is hot.

drill.title: Blind-bake a crust; stop a soggy bottom
body: Blind baking, and the soggy bottom it prevents, are easiest to understand side by side. If you're making the quiche, its crust is this drill. If you're making the patties, use a little of their pastry to bake two small test tarts.
steps: Making the quiche: follow its blind-bake steps, and stop to look at the crust after the weighted bake and again after the empty bake. Note the color and how the bottom feels.
Making the patties: roll two 4-inch rounds of their pastry and press each into a muffin cup or small ovenproof dish.
Blind-bake one: foil, weights or dried beans, 12 minutes at 400°F, then 5 minutes empty. Leave the other raw.
Fill both with 2 tablespoons of milk whisked with 1 tablespoon of beaten egg, and bake both 12 minutes at 350°F.
Cool them and cut both open. Compare the bottoms.
Write down what blind baking changed and why.

quiz.q: Which tart had the crisper bottom?
quiz.explain: It was set before the filling went in.

quiz.q: When are the weights taken out?
choices: After the crust is set, so the bottom can dry and brown

quiz.q: What color should a blind-baked crust be before filling?
choices: Dry and golden, with no shiny spots

knowledge.title: Blind baking and soggy bottoms
body: A soggy bottom is pastry that never got hot and dry enough to set before a wet filling soaked into it. The fixes all aim at the same thing: getting the bottom crust baked before, or faster than, the filling makes it wet.

Blind baking bakes the crust empty first. Lined with foil and filled with weights so the sides don't slump and the bottom doesn't puff, it bakes until set, then bakes unweighted until the bottom is dry and golden. For a custard filling like quiche, it's essential: the custard never gets hot enough to bake raw pastry under it.
A seal finishes the job. Brushing the hot, blind-baked crust with beaten egg and returning it for 2 minutes cooks a thin waterproof layer between pastry and filling.

Bottom heat helps every pie. Bake on the lowest rack, on a sheet pan heated in the oven, so heat hits the bottom first. Glass and dark metal pie plates brown the bottom faster than shiny ones. Cook watery fillings first (wilt and wring spinach, brown mushrooms dry), and keep juicy fruit fillings thickened.

This week's Explore dish is Jamaican. Jamaican cooking is built on thyme, allspice (called pimento there), Scotch bonnet pepper, green onion (escallion), and garlic, with curry from the Indian cooks who came to the island in the 1800s. The beef patty brings them together in a pastry that, in Jamaica, is often made with beef fat; this one uses butter.
steps: Cut a slice of this week's quiche or a patty in half and look at the bottom crust. Is it crisp and golden, or pale and damp? Draw it.
List the steps in this week's recipe that protect the bottom crust, and what each one does.
Write down the five base flavors of Jamaican cooking and which ones are in this week's patties.

quiz.q: What causes a soggy bottom?
choices: The filling wets the crust before it can set
quiz.explain: The bottom never got hot and dry enough.

quiz.q: Why are weights used in blind baking?
choices: To stop the sides slumping and the bottom puffing
To add weight to the pie
quiz.explain: Foil and weights hold the shape.

quiz.q: What does an egg seal do?
choices: Makes a waterproof layer between crust and filling
quiz.explain: Brush the hot crust and bake 2 minutes.

quiz.q: Why bake on a preheated sheet pan on the lowest rack?
choices: Heat hits the bottom crust first

quiz.q: What do Jamaicans call allspice?

sabbath.title: Make pastry ahead and freeze it
body: Pastry dough is the slow part of any pie, and it keeps beautifully. Made ahead and frozen, it turns a quiche or a batch of patties into an evening's work instead of an afternoon's, and a frozen blind-baked shell is a head start on next week's dinner.
steps: Make a double batch of this week's pastry. Press each half into a 1-inch disk.
Wrap each disk tightly in plastic wrap, then put them in a freezer bag. Label it with the kind of pastry and the date. It keeps 3 months.
Or roll one into the pie plate, crimp it, and freeze it in the plate, wrapped. It goes from the freezer straight into a blind bake, adding 5 minutes.
To use a disk, thaw it overnight in the fridge. It should feel cold but bend without cracking.
Note how long the frozen dough took, start to finish, compared with fresh.

quiz.q: How long does frozen pastry dough keep?
How do you thaw a disk?
choices: On the counter for an hour

quiz.q: Can a frozen crust in its plate be blind-baked from frozen?
quiz.explain: The cold helps it hold its shape.

drill.title: Scale a quick bread and time it to the main
body: Scaling and timing, done for real on this week's dish. You'll write the scaled recipe and a timeline before you cook, then check your plan against the clock.
steps: Decide how many your family needs this week. Scale this week's recipe to it, by weight, and write the new ingredient list.
List every step that takes time: chilling, browning, simmering, baking, resting. Give each its minutes.
Write a timeline backward from the time you'll serve, so the dish that can't wait finishes last.
Cook to your timeline. Note the real clock time at each step.
Afterward, compare the plan with the real times. Where did you lose or gain time? Write one change for next time.

quiz.q: Where does a cooking timeline start?
quiz.explain: The last step sets the rest.

quiz.q: What finishes last?
Why note the real times as you cook?
choices: To fix the plan next time

knowledge.title: Chemical leaveners at a larger batch
body: Scaling a quick bread looks like simple multiplication, and mostly it is. Weigh the flour, liquid, and fat, multiply, and the batch scales exactly. Measured by cups, every scoop's error multiplies too.

Leaveners need care. Up to a double batch, baking powder and baking soda scale with everything else. Beyond that, many bakers scale them slightly less, because a big batch sits longer before it's all in the oven and bubbles escape from the waiting dough. The rule of thumb for biscuits and scones is about 1 teaspoon of baking powder per cup of flour (5 ounces), and ¼ teaspoon of baking soda per ½ cup of buttermilk.

Baking time follows size, not batch. Twelve biscuits the same size as six bake in the same 13 minutes, as long as the pan isn't crowded. A loaf twice as big takes far longer than twice the time. When a batch fills two pans, bake them on two racks and swap them halfway.

Timing the bread to the main dish means working backward. Quick breads won't wait: biscuits flatten and arepas harden as they cool. Sauces, gravies, and stews will. So the dish that holds goes first, and the bread goes in the oven last, timed to come out as the plates do.

This week's Explore dish is Venezuelan. Venezuelan home cooking is built around the arepa, made every day from precooked corn flour, and stuffed with whatever's on hand: black beans (caraotas), white cheese, shredded beef, avocado. Cumin, garlic, onion, and sweet peppers are the base of its flavors.
steps: Scale this week's biscuit recipe to 18 biscuits by weight. Write the new amounts.
Check the baking powder against the rule of thumb. Is it close?
Write a timeline, backward from serving, for this week's recipe: when each part starts and ends.

quiz.q: Why scale by weight?
choices: Cup errors multiply with the batch

quiz.q: Twelve biscuits instead of six, the same size. The baking time…
Which goes first on a timeline: the biscuits or the gravy?
About how much baking powder per cup of flour in biscuits?
quiz.explain: A rule of thumb to check a recipe.

sabbath.title: Freeze unbaked biscuits
body: Biscuits freeze better unbaked than baked. Cut and frozen raw, they go straight into a hot oven and rise as tall as fresh ones, so a warm breakfast needs no mixing at all.
steps: Make and cut a batch of biscuits as this week's recipe says, but don't bake them.
Set them on a lined sheet pan, not touching, and freeze them until hard, about 2 hours.
Move them to a freezer bag, press out the air, and label it with the oven temperature and date. They keep 3 months.
To bake, don't thaw. Set them on a lined pan, sides touching, and bake at 450°F for 3 to 5 minutes longer than fresh, until tall and golden.
Bake one fresh and one frozen side by side if you can, and compare the height.

quiz.q: Do frozen biscuits need to thaw?
choices: No, bake them frozen, a few minutes longer

quiz.q: Why freeze them on a pan first?
choices: So they don't stick together in the bag
quiz.explain: Then take out just what you need.

quiz.q: How long do they keep?

drill.title: Weave a lattice; vent and crimp
body: A lattice is woven, not laid on, and its vents and crimp hold the pie together. You'll weave the lattice for this week's apple pie. Cooking the malva pudding instead? Practice the weave with ten 1-inch strips cut from a sheet of paper.
steps: Roll the top crust on parchment ⅛ inch thick and cut 10 strips, 1 inch wide, with a ruler for straight edges.
Lay 5 strips across the pie, evenly spaced, the longest in the middle.
Fold back strips 1, 3, and 5. Lay a strip across at a right angle near the edge. Unfold them.
Fold back strips 2 and 4. Lay the next cross strip. Unfold. Repeat until the top is woven.
Trim everything ½ inch past the rim. Fold the overhang under the bottom crust's edge.
Flute the edge: push the dough out with one finger from inside while pinching it with two from outside, all the way around.
Look at the gaps. They're the vents. Would a solid top need slits? Why?

quiz.q: How do you weave a lattice?
choices: Fold back every other strip, lay a cross strip, unfold, repeat
Lay all the strips on top of each other

quiz.q: Why does a solid top crust need slits?
quiz.explain: A lattice's gaps do the same job.

quiz.q: Why tuck the overhang under before fluting?
choices: It makes a thick edge that seals and holds its shape

knowledge.title: Fruit-pie thickeners; reading doneness by the bubbling
body: A fruit filling is fruit, sugar, and a thickener for the juice the fruit gives off. Each thickener behaves differently.

Cornstarch is cheap and strong and sets clear-ish, but only once it boils, and acid or long baking can weaken it. Use about 1 tablespoon per pound of fruit, more for juicy berries. Flour works too but needs about twice as much and makes a cloudier, pastier filling. Tapioca starch sets glossy and clear and holds up to freezing. Apples hold their own pectin, so they need the least.

Reading doneness by the bubbling: because starch thickens only at a boil, a fruit pie isn't done until the juice in the very center is bubbling thickly and slowly, not just the edges. Thin, fast bubbles mean it hasn't thickened yet. A thermometer in the center filling reads about 200°F when it's ready. Then the pie needs at least 2 hours to cool before the thickened juice sets enough to slice.
Juicy fruit can be managed before baking: sugared fruit gives off its juice in 30 minutes, and that juice can be boiled down to a syrup and returned, so less liquid ever reaches the crust.

This week's Explore dish is South African. Its home cooking mixes Dutch, Malay, Indian, and African traditions: bobotie and bredies, sambals and chutneys, and rich baked puddings like malva and milk tart, often finished with a pour of custard.
steps: Weigh this week's fruit and work out the cornstarch at 1 tablespoon per pound. Does it match the recipe?
Watch the pie's center bubbles near the end of baking. Write down what they looked like when it was done.
Write a short reflection: what you'd change about your mastery bake, and why it worked or didn't.

quiz.q: When does cornstarch thicken?
quiz.explain: That's why you wait for center bubbles.

quiz.q: About how much cornstarch per pound of fruit?
What do thick, slow bubbles in the center mean?
choices: The filling has thickened; the pie is done
quiz.explain: Thin, fast bubbles mean not yet.

quiz.q: Which thickener stays clear and freezes well?

sabbath.title: Leaven and unleavened bread (Exodus 12:15–20; 1 Corinthians 5:6–8)
body: Leaven is anything that makes dough rise by fermentation, or that lightens a batter with gas: yeast, a sourdough starter, baking powder and baking soda. You've baked with all of them this unit. Scripture uses leaven two ways, as a real food and as a picture.

As a food: Israel left Egypt so quickly that their dough had no time to rise, and they carried it out in their kneading bowls (Exodus 12:34, 39). God commanded unleavened bread for seven days each year, from the evening of the 14th day of the first month to the evening of the 21st, with all leaven removed from their houses (Exodus 12:15–20). Deuteronomy calls it "the bread of affliction" (Deuteronomy 16:3).

As a picture: "a little leaven leavens the whole lump" (1 Corinthians 5:6). Paul uses the way a pinch of starter works through a whole batch to show how one sin tolerated spreads through a community, and calls believers to keep the festival "with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth" (1 Corinthians 5:8). Jesus warned of "the leaven of the Pharisees," their teaching (Matthew 16:6–12).

Leaven isn't always bad. The two loaves of the Feast of Weeks were baked with leaven (Leviticus 23:17), and Jesus compared the kingdom of heaven to leaven worked through three measures of flour until all of it rose (Matthew 13:33). Families keep the unleavened days in different ways; this app shows the days a family sets and plans around leavened recipes on them.
steps: Read Exodus 12:14–20 and 12:33–39, and Deuteronomy 16:3.
Read 1 Corinthians 5:6–8 and Matthew 16:6–12.
Read Leviticus 23:15–17 and Matthew 13:33.
Go back through this unit's recipes and list which leavener each used: yeast, baking powder, baking soda, or none.
Write a short essay: how does leaven work in dough, and how do Paul and Jesus use that to teach? Use at least three passages.

quiz.q: Why was Israel's bread unleavened when they left Egypt?
choices: They left in haste, before the dough could rise

quiz.q: What does Deuteronomy 16:3 call unleavened bread?
quiz.explain: Eaten to remember leaving Egypt in haste.

quiz.q: What did Jesus mean by "the leaven of the Pharisees"?
Which offering was baked with leaven?
choices: The two loaves at the Feast of Weeks

drill.title: Hold a poaching liquid at 170–180°F
body: Holding a liquid in a narrow window is the skill behind poaching, custards, and sous vide. You'll hold a pan of water at 170–180°F for 15 minutes using only the burner and a thermometer. Use the court-bouillon pan from this week's recipe, or plain water.
steps: Fill a wide skillet with 2 inches of water and set the thermometer in it.
Bring it to 180°F, then turn the burner down.
Check every minute for 15 minutes. Write each reading and every burner change.
At minute 8, drop in a cup of cold water to imitate adding cold fish. Time how long it takes to recover to 170°F.
Graph your readings over time. What burner setting held the window best?

quiz.q: What did adding cold water do?
choices: Dropped the temperature, which then recovered

quiz.q: Why check every minute?
choices: Small burner changes take a minute or two to show

knowledge.title: Poaching vs. simmering: the temperatures
body: Boiling, simmering, and poaching are the same method at different temperatures, and each suits different food. Water boils at 212°F at sea level: big bubbles break hard across the surface. A simmer is about 185–205°F: small bubbles rise steadily and break gently. Poaching is 160–180°F: the surface barely moves, with only a few small bubbles on the bottom of the pan.

Delicate proteins need the lowest of these. Fish and eggs set between about 130°F and 160°F; held in 170–180°F liquid, the outside never races far ahead of the center, so the whole piece cooks evenly and stays moist. At a boil, the outer layer overcooks and squeezes out water and white albumin before the center is done, and the agitation breaks flakes apart.

Bubbles are a rough guide only; altitude, pan, and burner all change them. A thermometer in the liquid is the real control. Because adding cold food drops the temperature, start a few degrees high and adjust the burner as the liquid recovers. A wide pan holds a steady temperature better than a deep pot.

The liquid matters too. A court-bouillon (water with aromatics and acid) seasons fish from the outside; a curry or stock does the same with more body. Fat-rich liquids like coconut milk can split at a hard boil, another reason to keep poaching gentle.

This week's Explore dish is from Goa, on India's west coast, where fish curry and rice is the everyday meal. Goan cooking uses coconut in almost everything, sour tamarind or kokum to balance it, dried Kashmiri chiles for color more than heat, and a fresh masala ground for each dish.
steps: Heat a pan of water and use the thermometer to find the burner settings that hold 212°F, 195°F, and 175°F. Write them down.
Describe the surface of the water at each temperature.
List three foods you'd cook at each of the three temperatures, and why.

quiz.q: What temperature range is poaching?
Why poach fish rather than boil it?
choices: The outside doesn't overcook before the center

quiz.q: What's the real control for poaching temperature?
quiz.explain: Bubbles vary by pan and altitude.

quiz.q: Why start the liquid a few degrees high?
What balances coconut in Goan curry?

sabbath.title: Make a court-bouillon ahead
body: A court-bouillon takes 15 minutes to simmer, and that's most of the work in poaching fish. Made ahead and kept in the fridge, it turns poached fish into a 15-minute dinner.

Strain it, cool it quickly, and keep it covered in the fridge for up to 3 days or frozen for 3 months. Reheat it to 180°F before the fish goes in. Used once for fish, it's best thrown away: it carries the fish's proteins and spoils quickly.
steps: Make a double court-bouillon: water, onion, celery, carrot, lemon, bay leaves, peppercorns, parsley stems, and salt, simmered 15 minutes.
Strain it, cool it in an ice bath, and pack it into containers. Label and date them.
Later in the week, reheat one to 180°F and poach fish or eggs in it.
Write down the time from fridge to table.

quiz.q: How long does court-bouillon keep in the fridge?
Why not reuse it after poaching fish?
choices: It carries the fish's proteins and spoils quickly
